section_summary: This section covers political, diplomatic, and economic developments in Japan from December 1932 through February 1933 as reported by the U.S. Embassy in Tokyo under Ambassador Joseph C. Grew. It highlights Japan's escalating conflict with the League of Nations over Manchuria culminating in the Cabinet's decision to withdraw, military confrontations at Shanhaikwan and the advance into Jehol, and mounting military dominance over domestic politics and the national budget. The reports also trace Japanese-American relations—including labor unrest at the Singer Sewing Machine Company in Yokohama, espionage accusations, and reactions to the Philippine Independence bill—alongside financial developments such as the February 1933 stock market collapse.

subfiles.about: Concluding portion of the monthly report covering Japanese diplomatic, military, political, and economic developments in December 1932, along with records of Embassy communications.
subfiles.summary: The report discusses Japan's refusal to accept the draft resolution of the League's Committee of 19, the establishment of the Japanese Embassy in Manchukuo under General Nobuyoshi Muto, and military operations clearing anti-Japanese forces under General Su Ping-wen near Manchuli. It reviews border skirmishes at Shanhaikwan, reactions to the resumption of Sino-Soviet diplomatic ties, and Japan's proposals to the Disarmament Conference for naval reductions. Domestically, it covers the convening of the 64th Diet, cabinet stability under Premier Saito, the formation of Adachi's Kokumin Domei, banking reorganizations under the 1927 law, the Singer strike, and schedules of despatches and telegrams sent to Washington.
subfiles.title: Monthly Political Report for December 1932 (Report No. 75)

subfiles.about: Embassy despatch transmitting the monthly political and economic report on conditions in Japan for January 1933.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 278 transmits Report No. 76, highlighting the violent attack by strikers on the Singer Sewing Machine Company's Yokohama offices and official press allegations regarding American military assistance to China. It examines Japan's widening breach with the League of Nations, the military clash at Shanhaikwan, preparations for an advance into Jehol, and deteriorating relations with the Soviet Union following the collapse of non-aggression pact negotiations. The report also details Diet debates over large military appropriations, wholesale arrests of communists, the resignation of Tokyo Mayor Nagata, Finance Minister Takahashi's optimistic budget defense, and lists of despatches and telegrams sent during January.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 278: Monthly Report on Conditions in Japan during the Month of January, 1933 (Report No. 76)

subfiles.about: State Department briefing memorandum highlighting key foreign policy, military, and economic developments reported in Tokyo's monthly report for February 1933.
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State
subfiles.summary: Summarizes Grew's February 1933 report: Cabinet won on leaving the League over moderates' opposition; Young Officers League intimidation; military budgets unchallenged; Tokyo stock market collapse from February 14.
subfiles.title: Department of State Memorandum on Tokyo's Monthly Report for February 1933

subfiles.about: Embassy despatch transmitting the monthly political and economic report on conditions in Japan for February 1933, focusing on Japan's withdrawal from the League of Nations and the invasion of Jehol.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 309 transmits Report No. 77, recording the historic decision of the Japanese Cabinet on February 20, 1933, to withdraw from the League of Nations following the Assembly's adoption of the Committee of Nineteen report. It chronicles the military advance into Jehol, the amicable settlement of the Singer strike and the National City Bank espionage controversy, and an incident involving Soviet vessels in the Bonin Islands. Domestically, the report details political pressure from the Young Officers League and Blood Brotherhood League indictments, the return of liberal statesman Yukio Ozaki, Imperial Household changes, the passage of the budget and Exchange Control Law, and a sharp decline in the Tokyo stock market.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 309: Monthly Report on Conditions in Japan during the Month of February, 1933 (Report No. 77)
